name: Queen Victoria
info: Victoria (1819–1901) was Queen of the United Kingdom from 1837 and Empress of India from 1876, whose reign of more than 63 years gave its name to the Victorian era of industrial change and imperial expansion.

facts.born: 24 May 1819 at Kensington Palace, London; only child of Prince Edward, Duke of Kent and Strathearn, fourth son of George III, and Princess Victoria of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld
facts.died: 22 January 1901 at Osborne House on the Isle of Wight, aged 81, disabled by rheumatism and nearly blind with cataracts, in the presence of her son Albert Edward and grandson Wilhelm II
facts.role: Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland (20 June 1837 – 22 January 1901); Empress of India (from 1 May 1876); the last British monarch of the House of Hanover
facts.known: the longest British reign until 2015; her marriage to Prince Albert and their nine children, the 'grandmother of Europe'; the bedchamber crisis of 1839; long mourning and seclusion after 1861; the title Empress of India; the Golden and Diamond Jubilees of 1887 and 1897; the 'family monarchy'; her journals of 122 volumes

t: Raised in isolation under her mother's 'Kensington System', Victoria came to the throne at eighteen in 1837 and relied first on Lord Melbourne and then, after their marriage in 1840, on her husband Prince Albert.

She tried privately to sway policy and appointments, favouring Disraeli, loathing Gladstone and endorsing an expanding empire whose title of Empress of India she took in 1876, while the monarchy's formal power continued to pass to Parliament.

Her withdrawal after Albert's death in 1861 fed a republican movement, but by her Golden and Diamond Jubilees she was again widely popular, the matriarchal figure of a family monarchy and a world empire.
dyk: Victoria had chloroform for the birth of her son Leopold in 1853 and again for Beatrice's in 1857, despite clergy who called it against biblical teaching and doctors who thought it dangerous.
ev: Born at Kensington Palace, the only child of the Duke and Duchess of Kent
Becomes Queen of the United Kingdom on the death of her uncle William IV, less than a month after her 18th birthday
Marries her first cousin Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha in the Chapel Royal of St James's Palace
Albert dies of typhoid fever in December, and Victoria withdraws into mourning and seclusion
Takes the title Empress of India under the Royal Titles Act, proclaimed at the Delhi Durbar the next year
Celebrates her Golden Jubilee with a banquet for 50 kings and princes and a service in Westminster Abbey
Her Diamond Jubilee is held as a festival of the British Empire, with troops from all over the empire
Dies at Osborne House and is buried beside Albert at Frogmore

sections.early:
Victoria was born at Kensington Palace on 24 May 1819, the only child of Prince Edward, Duke of Kent, fourth son of George III, and of Princess Victoria of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld, a widowed German princess. Her birth followed the death in 1817 of Princess Charlotte, the king's only legitimate grandchild, which had pushed his unmarried sons to marry. She was christened Alexandrina, after her godfather Tsar Alexander I, and Victoria, after her mother. Her father died in January 1820 and her grandfather a week later, leaving her third in line behind her uncles Frederick and William. When Frederick died in 1827 and George IV in 1830, William IV became king and Victoria his heir presumptive.

She later called her childhood "rather melancholy". Her mother and her ambitious comptroller, Sir John Conroy, raised her under the "Kensington System", a set of rules that kept her from most of her father's family and was designed to leave her weak and dependent on them. She slept in her mother's room, studied French, German, Italian and Latin with tutors, and was taken on tours of England and Wales that annoyed the king, who saw them as royal progresses. She resisted every attempt to make Conroy her private secretary. In 1836 her uncle Leopold, King of the Belgians, brought his nephew Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha to visit; she wrote that he was "extremely handsome", though at seventeen she was not ready to marry.
sections.rise:
Victoria turned eighteen on 24 May 1837, so a regency was avoided, and on 20 June William IV died and she became queen. She dropped the name Alexandrina at once. Because Salic law barred women from the Hanoverian succession, the crown of Hanover passed to her uncle Ernest Augustus, ending the union of 1714. The Whig prime minister Lord Melbourne became a powerful influence on the inexperienced queen, who probably saw him as a father figure. She was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 28 June 1838, became the first sovereign to live at Buckingham Palace, and paid off her father's debts.

Her early popularity suffered in 1839. Believing rumours that her mother's lady-in-waiting Lady Flora Hastings was pregnant by Conroy, she was implicated in a press campaign when Lady Flora was found to be a virgin and, at her death that July, to have had a tumour on her liver; the queen was hissed in public as "Mrs. Melbourne". The same year, when Melbourne resigned and Robert Peel was asked to form a government, she refused to let him replace her Whig ladies of the bedchamber, and Peel declined to govern, returning Melbourne to office. She proposed to Albert on 15 October 1839 and married him on 10 February 1840. Albert replaced Melbourne as her chief adviser, and relations with her mother, whom she had kept at a distance, slowly improved through his mediation.
sections.deeds:
Victoria and Albert had nine children between 1840 and 1857, who married into royal and noble families across Europe. In politics the queen sought to influence ministers and appointments. She supported the repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846, quarrelled with Lord Palmerston for sending dispatches without her knowledge until he was removed in 1851, and worked to improve relations with France, becoming in 1843 the first British monarch to visit a French king since 1520 and in 1855 the first reigning British monarch in Paris in over 400 years. After the Indian Rebellion of 1857 she condemned atrocities on both sides and had the proclamation transferring India to the Crown promise religious freedom. She supported the Reform Act 1867, which doubled the electorate, though she was not in favour of votes for women.

She was charmed by Benjamin Disraeli, who said royalty should be flattered "with a trowel", and endorsed his expansionist policy, which led to the Anglo-Zulu War and the Second Anglo-Afghan War. His Royal Titles Act made her Empress of India from 1 May 1876, proclaimed at the Delhi Durbar of 1877. She saw the empire as civilising and benign, writing that Britain must be "Prepared for attacks and wars, somewhere or other, CONTINUALLY". She founded orders and decorations including the Victoria Cross in 1856, and in 1887 and 1897 her Golden and Diamond Jubilees became celebrations of the empire.
sections.opponents:
Victoria faced hostility at several points of her reign. In Ireland, where the Great Famine from 1845 killed over a million people and drove another million to emigrate, she was labelled "The Famine Queen". She gave £2,000 to the British Relief Association in 1847, more than any other individual donor; the story that she gave only £5 was a myth of the late 19th century. Her long seclusion after 1861 diminished the monarchy's popularity: in 1864 a protester posted a notice that Buckingham Palace was to be let or sold, and in 1870, after the founding of the Third French Republic, a rally in Trafalgar Square demanded her removal. Her reliance on John Brown, a manservant from Scotland, and later on her Indian secretary Abdul Karim, the Munshi, drew gossip and her household's anger; she dismissed the complaints about Karim as racial prejudice. She was also the target of several attempts on her life, by Edward Oxford in 1840 and others up to Roderick Maclean in 1882.

She in turn opposed ministers. Gladstone spoke to her, she is thought to have complained, as though she were "a public meeting rather than a woman"; she called his government "the worst I have ever had", blamed him for General Gordon's death at Khartoum and was gleeful when his Irish home rule bill was defeated. Between 1877 and 1878 she threatened five times to abdicate to push Disraeli against Russia, without effect. Her biographers conclude that she was emotional, obstinate, honest and straight-talking.
sections.last:
In her last decades Victoria lost several of her children. Her daughter Alice died of diphtheria on 14 December 1878, the anniversary of Albert's death, and her son Leopold, who had haemophilia, in 1884. A fall at Windsor in 1883 left her lame and troubled by rheumatism thereafter. Her eldest daughter was widowed in 1888 after a little over three months as German empress, and her grandson became Emperor Wilhelm II, whose autocratic views ended her and Albert's hopes of a liberal Germany. On 23 September 1896 she passed George III as the longest-reigning monarch in British history. At the Diamond Jubilee of 22 June 1897 she sat in her open carriage outside St Paul's Cathedral for the service of thanksgiving.

With the Boer War unpopular in Europe, she visited Ireland in 1900 for the first time since 1861, partly to honour its regiments. Her son Alfred died that July. She spent Christmas 1900 at Osborne House, as she did throughout her widowhood, disabled by rheumatism and with cataracts clouding her sight, and by mid-January she was drowsy and confused. She died there on 22 January 1901, aged 81, with her son Albert Edward and Wilhelm II present, and Albert Edward succeeded as Edward VII. Following her own instructions she had a military and white funeral, and was buried beside Albert in the Royal Mausoleum at Frogmore.
sections.legacy:
Victoria's reign of 63 years, seven months and two days was the longest of any British monarch, and of any queen regnant in world history, until Elizabeth II passed it in 2015. She was the last of the House of Hanover. Through her nine children she became "the grandmother of Europe"; 34 grandchildren survived to adulthood, and the haemophilia carried by her descendants appeared in the royal houses of Russia and Spain. Modern speculation that her real father was not the Duke of Kent has no documentary support, and a spontaneous mutation, more common in the children of older fathers, is thought more likely.

During her reign the modern constitutional monarchy took shape, as reforms of the vote increased the power of the Commons at the expense of the Lords and the Crown; in 1867 Walter Bagehot wrote that the monarch kept only "the right to be consulted, the right to encourage, and the right to warn". Only after her diaries and letters were published did the extent of her political influence become widely known. Her emphasis on morality and family life, against the scandals of earlier members of the House of Hanover, made the "family monarchy" one the middle classes could identify with. Early biographies such as Lytton Strachey's of 1921 are now considered out of date; those of Elizabeth Longford, Cecil Woodham-Smith and Stanley Weintraub are still admired.

summary: Victoria reigned over the United Kingdom from 1837 to 1901 and became Empress of India in 1876, presiding over an era of industrial change and imperial expansion. Privately she tried to steer ministers; publicly she became a symbol of personal morality and, after a long and unpopular seclusion following Prince Albert's death, the matriarch of a family monarchy and of Europe's royal houses.

notes: The article gives no figures for the Anglo-Zulu or Second Anglo-Afghan wars; the opponents section therefore turns on the Famine, republicanism and her quarrels with ministers rather than on imperial casualties.
Gladstone complaint is 'she is thought to have complained' in the article; kept the hedge.
Lady Flora Hastings: 'implicated in a press campaign' follows the article's 'organised a press campaign implicating the Queen'.
The diaries: Beatrice transcribed and burned the originals from the accession onwards; left out for length.
The 1876 title: the article says Parliament voted it in 1876 and she took it from 1 May 1876; Delhi Durbar 1 January 1877.
